page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Apply the property with a=π
steps.margin_note: First mark. cos(π−x) = −cosx, so cos³(π−x) = −cos³x — an odd power carries the sign through.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π−x)=sinx (unchanged); cos(π−x)=−cosx (sign flips) — always know both halves of this pair.
lines: By x → π−x: I = ∫₀^π sin³(π−x) cos³(π−x) dx
∴ I = ∫₀^π sin³x (−cosx)³ dx = −∫₀^π sin³x cos³x dx = −I
steps.why: Under x→π−x, sinx stays unchanged but cosx flips sign, so cos³x also flips sign (an odd power keeps the sign flip), giving the negative of the original integral.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that cos(π−x) = −cosx, and treating cos³(π−x) as +cos³x.
Applying the property x→π−x to the wrong integral.

steps.label: Add and solve for I
steps.margin_note: Second mark. I = −I is only possible if I = 0 — a short, direct conclusion.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever a property gives I = −I, the answer is always 0, with no further computation needed.
steps.why: Since the property shows I equals its own negative, adding I to both sides gives 2I=0, so the integral must be exactly zero.
common_mistakes: Concluding I is undefined instead of recognising I=0 is a valid, clean result.
Subtracting I from both sides instead of adding it, which loses the information.
